title: Two places, one James?
standfirst: George of Mureistoun is now James’s preferred probable father, with Andrew retained as an uncertain alternative. The same-holding/witness argument is stronger than the broader Calder placement; George’s merchant identity and upstream route remain uncertain.

status.label: Documented household; probable older profile matches

question: Do the Mid Calder and Inveresk baptisms belong to the same James?
answer: Preferred Edinburgh identity: the Duffe husband probably is the older1641/1649 weaver70%, supporting Robert as probable father61%; retain both accounts, younger alternatives and independent maternal assessments. Prefer the recorded Mureistoun George as James’s probable father from the combined 1586 locality and 1605 baptism-witness household. This does not resolve James’s Mid Calder/Inveresk identity, the merchant George comparison, or the upstream William route. The Fisherrow couple and child-role assessments remain as separately graded.

chapters.title: Edinburgh: the Duffe father probably is the older weaver
body: Research rationale: connect the Duffe family to the earlier Duddingston weaver family by assessing the entire craft, civic-status and successive-wife sequence, rather than preferring a younger generation merely because of a guessed birth year.

James Glasgow-2682, father of the Edinburgh Duffe household, probably represents the same adult as James Glasgow-1150, the weaver apprenticed on 16 June 1641 and admitted burgess on 20 June 1649: 70% subjective identity confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 youngest-son Thomas apprenticeships name a father James Glasgow, weaver and burgess of Edinburgh. Thomas’s maintained 1684 baptismal identification and the Duffe household’s James children of 1679 and 1680 fit those apprenticeship ages and the youngest-son order. The older craftsman independently has that specific craft and civic status, with an exact master/date cross-reference between his 1641 apprenticeship and 1649 admission. The maintained admission review found one matching admission, although this does not establish uniqueness. His marriages to Bessie Whyte on 6 July 1649 and Agnes Duncan on 11 November 1653, followed by Agnes’s burial as the weaver’s wife on 21 January 1674, permit a later Duffe household beginning in 1677. Successive marriages explain the wife sequence without requiring another same-name weaver and burgess.

Select Robert Glasgow-1156 as James-2682’s probable working father at 61%, conditional on that preferred adult identity and the existing 86% identification of the 1641 apprentice’s named father Robert with the Duddingston account buried in 1647. This replaces only the former local Johnne Glasgow-1151 hypothesis, retained unselected at 26%. The live father was blank in the public check on 21 October 2026: the outstanding WikiTree action is a new probable father addition, not replacement of a live father. The 61% and 70% are subjective assessments of nested propositions, not independent confirmations or statistically calculated probabilities.

The main weaknesses are a very long working life and late fatherhood through 1691, together with the absence of a marriage, prior-wife clause, address, witness or admission-date reference directly joining the Duffe husband to the 1649 burgess. The 1693 same-name weaver master is an inferred identification, not an independently dated identity bridge. Another younger Edinburgh weaver and burgess remains possible. The cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship could concern the 1696 son, but its deceased father would conflict with assigning that father to the living 1693 master; resolve this before a merge. Retain both James profiles as accounts of potentially one adult, not two proved sons of Robert. Johnne-1151 remains an unselected younger-family alternative at 26%, alongside the James-3076/James-3077 and Annapill Glessie childhood route, John-1084’s Gordon family, and an unrecorded father. Those alternatives are conditional on the Duffe husband being a distinct younger man, not equally compatible with the preferred pre-1641 adult.

The circa-1655 birth, previously inferred from the first known child in 1677, is a creation estimate rather than an age or birth record. The preferred older-adult identity independently supports birth before 16 June 1641, uncertain and conditional on that identity. Replace the local preferred estimate with that boundary, retaining the old circa-1655 and “by about 1657” reasoning as superseded history. This is a separate vital/identity correction, not a date altered solely to fit Robert’s 1647 burial. No exact birth year is established; retain the broad Midlothian birthplace without claiming a new birthplace record.

No mother is selected for James-2682; do not transfer Deborah Ivey or any wife of Robert from the older profile. Robert’s own 28% Corsoun father hypothesis and the older James’s 86% Robert link are unchanged. The 1696 apprentice’s selected father James-2682 remains 82%, probable mother Duffe-18 remains 72%, and brother comparison remains 79%. The two childhood James accounts stay separate. This is a reassessment of held evidence, with no new source discovery, original inspection, profile merger, live edit or confident upgrade. Connectivity counts still describe retained profile accounts and cannot establish their distinctness.

The most useful test is an Edinburgh marriage, guild, property, witness or prior-wife clause linking the Duffe husband to the 1649 burgess. Check the original 1690 cancelled indenture against the 1693 master before identifying that son or merging either James account; inspect the original Duffe baptisms for residence and witnesses. These are targeted next tests, not prerequisites to representing the preferred probable family.

chapters.title: Edinburgh apprentice brothers: James and Thomas, probable 79%
body: Current maternal assessment, 21 October 2026: Isobell/Elizabeth Duffe (Duffe-18) is now the selected probable mother of the 1696 apprentice James-4114 at 72%, through the qualified Duffe household. This supersedes the earlier decision below to leave his mother unselected. The 1679 Elizabeth and 1680 Issobell entries may name different women, and neither child is identified as the apprentice. Father82% and brother79% are unchanged; this is one new maternal hypothesis, not a new paternal join. See the full argument and original index locators in the linked maternal account.
Research rationale: link the late Edinburgh apprentice families while testing whether their father has two profile accounts.

James Glasgow-4114, apprenticed to William Adam, apothecary, on 22 April 1696, and Thomas Glasgow-3285, assigned to the baxter apprenticeship of 11 October 1699, are selected as probable brothers at 79% subjective confidence. Both entries name their father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess of Edinburgh. The matching personal name, craft and civic status, in the same register only three years apart, favour one father. Thomas is expressly the youngest son. His 13 November 1684 baptism fits entry at almost fifteen, while the Duffe household has sons James baptised in 1679 and 1680, fitting the 1696 entry at about seventeen or sixteen. This is a coherent sibling group rather than a name-only regional comparison.

The 79% assesses the profile-to-profile sibling inference, not a literal brother clause or measured frequency. The apprentice entries do not name a mother, address or the father’s admission date; two matching craftsmen remain possible. Thomas’s apprenticeship-to-baptism identity is a maintained assignment, supported by age and locality rather than a repeated birth date. Do not choose between the 1679 and 1680 James children, merge either with James-4114, or transfer Isobell Duffe as his mother. The 1690 Lindsayland apprentice James-4131 remains a compatible comparison, including the possibility of a cancelled first apprenticeship. If that identity is established, its deceased father must be reconciled with the master appearing in 1693.

The printed Greyfriars register records Agnes Duncan, wife of James Glasgow, weaver, buried on 21 January 1674 (printed pp.196 and 252; PDF pp.212 and 268, visually checked). This fits the wife married in 1653 and removes a supposed overlapping-wife obstacle to identifying the older weaver James-1150 with the Duffe husband James-2682, whose known children begin in 1677. Different wives alone do not exclude successive marriages. The same surname page records an unnamed stillborn child of James the weaver on 16 January 1687 and another unnamed child on 18 March 1690. Neither is assigned to a named baptismal child or mother.

Earlier selection, superseded21October2026 for the Duffe husband only: James-1150 and James-2682 remain compatible accounts of possibly one adult. James-2682’s circa-1655 birth is an estimate from his first known child, not an age record excluding the older man. The older craftsman’s long career and the late Duffe family are compatible, though fatherhood continuing to 1691 would be late. No marriage, wife clause or address ties the Duffe household directly to the 1649 burgess. Retain both accounts and recorded families while testing that identity. The 20 October review prefers the Duffe father account for James-4114 at82%, with James-1150’s earlier76% selection retained as a compatible same-adult alternative; James-2682’s Johnne-1151 placement stays speculative 26%, conditional on a distinct younger identity. These are different propositions, not independent corroboration. No live parent replacement, new mother, vital change or identity merger is selected; the local father preference is revised. Current conclusion: older-weaver identity70%, Robert-1156 father61%; Johnne remains alternative26%. The Kirknewton William route is unchanged.

The useful next discriminator is a weavers’ incorporation, testament or baptismal original giving the Duffe husband’s trade, address or prior marriage. A further same-name hit without such detail will not distinguish the adult accounts. The 1701–1760 burgess PDF at Trades House starts with Hepburn and cannot establish absence under Glasgow. The maintained 30 September ScotsFind transcript review covers that missing surname section, but the original Part I page remains uninspected.

Earlier selection, superseded21October2026 for the Duffe husband only: 20 October 2026: Prefer James Glasgow-2682, the father account defined by the Edinburgh Duffe household, as the 1696 apothecary apprentice James Glasgow-4114’s probable father at 82% subjective confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 Thomas entries name their father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Thomas’s maintained identification with the 13 November 1684 child of James and Isobell Duffe gives an entry age of almost fifteen. The household’s James children of 16 March 1679 and 18 April 1680 fit the 1696 entry at seventeen or sixteen. Thomas is the youngest recorded son in this family, consistent with the 1699 indenture’s youngest-son description; the later recorded child, Margaret in 1691, is a daughter. This household-specific age and sibling order gives a better father-profile fit than selecting the older craftsman solely through the repeated occupational description. The James-1150 account remains compatible as another account of this same adult, not an excluded or necessarily different biological father. The 82% assesses the complete father-profile proposition, including Thomas’s inferred apprentice-to-baptism identity and the inferred common father. These clues are related and are considered together, not multiplied as independent confirmations. Neither apprentice entry names a mother, address, father’s admission date or birth date. Another matching family remains possible. The 1679 mother’s Elizabeth/Isobell attribution is retained with its existing qualification. The 1679 and 1680 James profiles remain separate, and neither is selected as the apprentice or Jean Dobie’s husband. Isobell Duffe is not assigned as James-4114’s mother. The possible cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship remains unresolved; its father was deceased, while a same-name Edinburgh master appears in 1693. The 1691 baptism alone does not prove its father alive. James-2682’s speculative Johnne-1151 ancestry at 26%, James-1150’s probable Robert-1156 ancestry at 86%, and all vital fields are unchanged. This is a revised local selection; the live father remains blank, so the pending WikiTree action is a new father addition, not replacement of a live parent. The sibling assessment remains 79%. Current conclusion: older-weaver identity70%, Robert-1156 father61%; Johnne remains alternative26%. The Kirknewton William route is unchanged.

Maternal review, 21 October 2026. Select Isobell/Elizabeth Duffe (Duffe-18) as James Glasgow-4114’s probable working mother at 72% subjective confidence, through the preferred Edinburgh Duffe household. The 1696 apothecary apprentice and the 1699 youngest-son apprentice Thomas share the specific father description James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Thomas’s maintained identification with the 1684 child of James and Isobell Duffe fits entry at almost fifteen. The supplied Edinburgh index gives a James to James Glasgow and Elizabeth Duffe on 16 March 1679, and another to James Glasgow and Issobell Duff on 18 April 1680. Either child fits the 1696 apprentice at seventeen or sixteen. Both childhood candidates therefore lead into a Duffe maternal household without requiring us to choose or merge the children.

No mother is named in either apprenticeship, and neither James baptism is securely identified with the apprentice. The two maternal forenames may represent different women; Duffe-18 is retained as the existing qualified Isobell/Elizabeth household account, not proof that those names denote one woman. The later James may be the survivor, but no infant burial proves that. Another matching craftsman’s family, a half-brother relationship, another Duffe woman, and the unresolved cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship remain alternatives. The 72% rates this whole maternal identification and stays below the father’s 82%; the father, brother and mother assessments share evidence and must not be multiplied as independent support.

This changes the earlier decision not to select a mother: use a probable household-level maternal hypothesis instead of leaving both compatible childhood routes unrepresented. The selected father James-2682 stays 82%, the compatible James-1150 alternative stays 76%, and the sibling comparison stays 79%. No childhood identity, birth/death date, spouse, existing child’s parent, upstream ancestry, merge or live WikiTree edit changes. One new local mother link is added; no paternal component or paternal-connectivity score improves.

Inspect the original 1679/1680 baptisms for maternal forenames, residence and witnesses, and seek an infant burial or later apprenticeship/occupation identifier. Compare the 1690 cancellation before any child-profile merger. The mother remains a probable proposal, not a documented maternal role of the apprentice.

chapters.title: Hugh’s 137-profile branch: prefer the local Corsankell family
body: Prefer John Glasgow-3193 of the Corsankell/Kilwinning family as Hugh Glasgow-1603’s uncertain working father. This materializes the leading Ayrshire placement already argued in the maintained five-generation map. The 1571 Corsinkell deed expressly names John as James elder’s son; the earlier Kilwinning tenant appearances are attributed to him as probable. Hugh’s surviving profile account describes an Ayrshire progenitor, his son’s account is centred on Kilwinning, and the following households lie in Kilwinning, Ayr and Kilbirnie. These successive local settings favour the documented nearby family over the existing Mid Calder/Inveresk father attachment, which depends on an online tree and has no movement, household or property bridge. A John-to-Hugh-to-John sequence is compatible supporting context, not a naming rule. Father is selected as a revisable one-generation model, rather than leaving the previously preferred local route only in prose.

Hugh remains a tree-derived generation: no inspected contemporary record securely identifies him, names his father or establishes his own c.1600 birth. John’s before-1540 boundary means a birth for Hugh near 1600 would make him an older father, around 60 or more; a grandson or collateral position may fit better. Neither date is changed to fit. An earlier Hugh birth is possible but is not adopted as a new estimate, and no missing person is invented. The 1571 John is documented as a son, while his additional Kilwinning identity is only probable. John’s brother James Glasgow-3921, another local Glasgow family, an omitted generation and the former James Glasgow-991 placement remain alternatives. This is stronger locality reasoning, not a probable or proved father assessment. The 1677 deed-index Hugh, preacher of the gospel, remains an unresolved identity comparison and supplies no evidence for this father choice.

The existing 137-profile pre-1850 working child side is rerouted from James of Mid Calder to John of Corsankell; descendants retain every earlier identity and relationship qualification. No mother, spouse, merge, new person or changed vital field is selected. Hugh-to-John-1604 and the minister’s separate father and duplicate questions are unchanged. Shared Y-DNA can motivate the extended-family model but cannot identify this father. Both proposed fathers already belong to the same working component: cohort membership, working component and pair coverage, supported connectivity and confidently marked connectivity remain unchanged. This is a better-supported placement within the working tree, not a newly connected component or confidence upgrade. No new source inspection or live WikiTree save is claimed.

The earlier Murieston father-review impact was 216 profiles below James. Rerouting Hugh’s 137-profile branch leaves 79 below James in the current pre-1850 working model; these are dated profile-impact counts, not changes in population or proofs of descent.

chapters.title: Murieston: a probable George father for James’s large branch
body: Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as James Glasgow-991’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule.

The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father.

For the working tree only, select William Glasgow-3522 as George of Mureistoun’s uncertain father through the surviving possible identification with the Glasgow merchant George Glasgow-1099. Protocol 2903 explicitly names that merchant’s deceased father William; protocol 2916 gives his mother and curator. The same rare full name and compatible 1586 generation make the merchant an existing-profile comparison for the Mureistoun man. The father proof belongs to the merchant: transferring it to the Mureistoun account depends entirely on the unproved identity. This is a testable named upstream route, not direct evidence of a Calder-to-Glasgow movement or a newly proved son of William.

The merchant was a minor in 1586, with the accepted approximate birth range 1565–1572. If James’s conventional circa-1575 birth were established, that would conflict with his being the merchant’s son. James’s birth is unrecorded: a later birth in the 1580s can fit the 1605 fatherhood and, toward the earlier end of George’s range, ordinary fatherhood in the previous generation. Those are compatibility examples, not new birth estimates. The 1598 marriage-contract comparison does not prove a first marriage or identify James’s mother. No date is altered to make this route fit. George-1099 stays a compatible candidate; there is no merge, no second distinct George son claimed for William, and no automatic transfer of Margaret Herbesoun or a wife as mother. If the two Georges are different men, William’s upstream placement must be reconsidered. The retained George Glascoe-36 and George-3171 comparisons remain open on their actual source limits.

James’s former selected Andrew father becomes an uncertain alternative; George of Mureistoun becomes the preferred probable father. A separately uncertain William upstream link keeps the family model inspectable. The record-only George uses the existing complete sourced public subject account and is not a new WikiTree profile or an independently counted extra surname person. The 216-profile pre-1850 child side below James retains all its downstream uncertainty and possible duplicates. The working cohort’s connected components and connected pairs do not improve merely because this named intermediary is displayed. No live WikiTree save, new original inspection, mother, birth/death change or certainty upgrade is claimed.

20October2026: Prefer the recorded George of Mureistoun as Edward Glasgow-1557’s uncertain working father at 26%, replacing the 18% Corsankell James selection. The preferred reconstruction makes Edward and James Glasgow-991 brothers. The 1624 Fisherrow index places Edward at the same RS25 9/135 reference as James the tailor and his son Alexander. Edward-1557 is the preferred 1624 identity at 56%; both Edward and the James family have Inveresk children in 1609, and James’s child Eduard supplies a compatible naming echo. A close local family explains this combined association better than the present unsupported Ayrshire-origin route. George is an already recorded older local candidate and James’s selected probable father at 82%; he is not an invented common ancestor. Brothers are the preferred degree for the two contemporary fathers, rather than a proved relationship. The 26% is an exact subjective assessment of the complete father-and-identity proposition, not a measured probability. Edward’s identity in 1624, James’s Mid Calder–Fisherrow identity, their precise degree of kinship and George’s paternity all remain open. The index gives Edward no capacity or kin clause; shared folio, local births and naming are correlated clues, not independent proofs. Cousins, uncle/nephew, an older Edward as James’s father, and another local father remain alternatives. Eduard-994 and Edward-1558 survive as the indexed Edward. The circa 1570/1575 birth years are estimates; if George is the merchant born 1565–1572, fatherhood requires later births for Edward and James, not those conventional estimates. No dates are changed to force that route. George’s own William-3522 father 26% and possible merchant identity are unchanged. Margaret Smith remains the separately uncertain imported mother; she is not selected as George’s spouse. No biological exclusion of Corsankell James or new Scottish–American proof is claimed.

21 October2026: the missing Berwick citation is recovered. Geo Glascoe was buried at Holy Trinity, Berwick upon Tweed, Northumberland, on 3 July 1589. The name, parish and exact date identify the existing George Glascoe-36 account. This is a burial date, not an exact death date. The transcript supplies no age, relatives or occupation; its synthetic birth-range search fields are not recorded ages or birth evidence. Scottish origin and named parentage remain unproved. The indexed burial excludes this George from the adult baptism-witness role at Mid Calder in 1605 and from the combined 1586–1605 identity. It does not exclude his being the Mureistoun man of 1586 alone. The merchant George Glasgow-1099 and George Glasgow-3171 retain their existing assessments. The selected Mureistoun George → James Glasgow-991 father remains 82%; William Glasgow-3522 → Mureistoun George remains 26%. No family link or percentage changes.

chapters.title: Fisherrow: two linked couples and the Inveresk children
body: Prefer the existing [James Glasgow](/people/glasgow-991.html) and [Christina Bie](/people/bie-55.html) family account for the Fisherrow James and Christina Bye. The printed 1624–1625 index explicitly groups James, tailor in Fisherrow and burgess of Musselburgh, his son Alexander and wife Christina Bye; it separately names Alexander’s wife Janet Clerk. Those are the same named family roles already represented by these profiles. The local James account also includes the Inveresk father sequence of 1609–1618, which can continue into the Fisherrow household. The ordinary Bye/Bie spelling and the full family fit make the identification probable, rather than a match resting only on James’s forename. This is an assessment of the preferred existing family account, not independent confirmation from its copied tree fields.

The printed sasine index places Janet Clerk with Alexander, while Christina Bye belongs with his father James. The 1637 Inveresk entry explicitly names Alexander Glasgow and Jannet Clerk as parents of their indexed son. The matching named couple and compatible 1624–1637 parish/property sequence document Alexander and Janet’s spouse relationship; no marriage ceremony date is supplied.

The Inveresk entries name Alexander Glasgow as father of Marioune in 1630, Johnne in 1632 and Bessie in 1635. They fall within the 1626–1637 series already represented by the Fisherrow Alexander’s family. The 1624–1625 sasines identify his wife Janet Clerk, and the 1637 child entry repeats that parental pair. The repeated father, parish, ordered child series and independently named couple strongly support this Alexander as the father in all three entries. This is confident family reconstruction from the combined records, not an assertion that each earlier entry names his occupation or wife.

The Mid Calder and Inveresk baptism sequences may still represent one mobile father or two contemporaries; no occupation or property recital joins them. The profile’s birth and death places remain inherited claims. The signed-in FamilySearch record VQ4V-K87 was inspected on 17 October 2026: it names William, father James and the 10 July 1614 Inveresk event, but no mother. It therefore supplies no independent evidence for Christina Bie’s maternity, consistent with the FMP and supplied ScotlandsPeople entries. The earlier citation-based claim that this record named her is withdrawn; the underlying parish image remains uninspected. Christina’s 1589 New Aberdour birth is tree-derived. Naming her as James’s wife in 1624 does not establish her as Alexander’s or William’s mother. The Andrew-3163 and Murieston-George ancestry alternatives retain their grades.

No mother is named in the three reviewed child entries, so their maternal grades stay unchanged. Bessie’s 22 March index date and existing 20 March birth field remain unreconciled; no date is changed. The later identities of these children, James-3923 versus the Edinburgh weaver James-1150, and the Edward property associations remain separate. Existing confident father settings for James-3923, Robert-1149 and Allexander-1152 are retained, not counted as new upgrades. Original sasines and parish images were not newly inspected.

Six existing assessments are strengthened: Alexander’s father and James’s Christina spouse identity become probable; Alexander and Janet’s marriage is documented; three previously ungraded fathers become strongly supported. The four paternal grade changes enter the probable-or-stronger graph, three of them the confident graph. No person, parent ID, maternal grade, date, selected working parent or live certainty flag changes. The existing pre-1850 child side below Alexander contains 24 profile accounts; downstream uncertainty remains explicit.

chapters.title: Murieston: George’s 1586–1605 identity is probable
body: Assessment history: the 17 October Murieston preferred-father review above supersedes the earlier selection of Andrew as James’s father. George of Mureistoun is now preferred, probable; Andrew remains an uncertain alternative. The earlier source readings and limits below are retained.

The preferred working identification is that George Glasgw in Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder muster obligation was the adult George Glasgow who witnessed the 17 February 1605 baptism of George, son of James Glasgow in provisionally read Muirestoun. The 1605 household points to the same holding as the earlier George, within the same parish setting. The surname is specific to this local comparison, and a 19-year interval is straightforward for one adult career. A child bearing George’s name and an adult George participating in his baptism make a continuing local family association more economical than two unconnected Georges. Together these observations warrant probable rather than merely possible cross-record identity. They do not amount to independent proofs of every step.

The witness’s own residence is unstated, and another George in the district remains possible. The residence reading Muirestoun and its identification as Murieston remain probable. Shared spelling and locality are related observations; McCall repeats Maidment’s 1586 act and is not a second muster occurrence. Naming the child George is supporting context, not proof of a naming rule. The 1586 act records an obligation, not attendance. Neither source gives George’s age or states a relationship to James. Father, uncle, brother, other kinsman and neighbour remain alternatives. No father is changed: Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains James’s selected uncertain father, while George is an important competing paternal or collateral explanation. George Glasgow-1099, the merchant, remains compatible but unselected; the 1586 minor’s curatorship and the 1598 marriage contract do not identify him at Murieston. No mother, birth date, identity merge or confidently marked paternal edge is added.

This improves a specific identity assessment within the 216-profile James branch, rather than raising Andrew’s father grade. The earlier possible assessment is retained as history. The working tree, confident paternal graph and fixed cohort are unchanged. The underlying 1605 register page was freshly inspected for this review; the 1586 printed-page verification from 15 October is retained, and the court manuscript remains unread.

chapters.title: Four selected working connections
body: Assessment history: the 17 October Murieston preferred-father review above supersedes the earlier selection of Andrew as James’s father. George of Mureistoun is now preferred, probable; Andrew remains an uncertain alternative. The earlier source readings and limits below are retained.

The local working tree now selects Andrew of Calder as tentative father of James, John of Linlithgow and David of Mid Calder. It selects the older Mid Calder/Quothquan John as tentative father of the1640s Kirknewton John. These are logical reconstructions from material already on this site, not newly discovered parentage records.

James Glasgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Andrew’s documented rural Calder household is the preferred working anchor for James’s nearby Mid Calder family. He was alive across the estimated1575–1586 birth interval of all three Lothian fathers; Hermand John’s1577 death would require an earlier birth estimate for David. That favours this coherent provisional family without excluding the other father. Andrew was alive until1598 and the uncertain generations allow James to be an older son. This uses the actual Calder setting and compatible family sequence, not the withdrawn assertion that the testament named James. James’s Inveresk/Fisherrow identity remains a separate uncertainty. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is another plausible older local father. The George named at Mureistoun1586 and the George witness1605 are a competing father/relative lead; identifying that George with merchant1099 would require additional identity assumptions and young fatherhood. None is excluded. Andrew’s omission of James weakens this model; it does not disprove an older son.

John Glasgow of Linlithgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Select the same older Calder household as the working origin for this neighbouring Lothian family. John’s estimated1579 generation and children recorded1613–1622 fit an older son of Andrew, whose own father is tentatively John-1093. The proximity and compatible generations make this a useful shared-family model alongside James and David, rather than an assertion that the three are proved brothers. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is a compatible alternative if John1561’s estimated birth is earlier than1577. A separate unnamed local father remains possible. Andrew’s1598 testament does not name John; do not restore the obsolete James/Andrew/William child list or attach Jonet Anderson as mother.

David Glasgow of Mid Calder → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: David’s1606 and1612 Mid Calder baptisms place his household in the same small Calder area as the earlier Andrew household. His approximate generation permits Andrew to be his father. The first recorded daughter Elspeth is consistent with the Elizat name in Andrew’s household, a minor naming clue rather than a mother identification. Select Andrew as the tentative shared father with James and John; exact birth years remain estimates. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 or another older local Glasgow could be the father. If David’s approximate1586 birth were established, he would have been young when omitted from Andrew’s1598 testament, making that omission more troublesome. It is not an established birth date. Elizat Stevinsoun and the discredited Jonet Anderson attribution are not automatically assigned as mothers.

John Glasgow of Kirknewton → John Glasgow, Mid Calder/Quothquan working identity: The older John already represents the father named in Mid Calder baptisms1608–1609. His son John-1086, baptised1608, is a viable earlier identity for the adult John who had children in neighbouring Kirknewton/East Calder1646–1650: age38 at the1646 birth is straightforward. Select the older John as working father of3610 on that local and chronological reconstruction. Keep the two son profiles separate while testing their possible identity. Alternatives: John-1086 has a later Biggar account that has not been equated with3610. They may be different men, and the older father’s Mid Calder/Montfoid/Quothquan identity is itself uncertain. Robert-4006 is another generationally compatible Calder father. This does not restore the former unsupported William-1087 father or treat1629 as a recorded birthday.
All four edges are uncertain and count only in the working pedigree. Confident relationships, raw WikiTree parent fields and the fixed cohort are unchanged. No mother is assigned by these selections.
